content: Keratosis pilaris (KP) is a prevalent genetic condition affecting the hair follicles, characterized by the presence of rough, small bumps on the skin. This condition is often colloquially referred to as chicken skin. It most commonly appears on the back and outer sides of the upper arms, though it can also affect the lower arms, thighs, tops of the legs, flanks, and buttocks. It can occur on any part of the body except for glabrous skin, such as the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. In less common cases, lesions may appear on the face, where they are sometimes mistaken for acne. Globally, keratosis pilaris affects an estimated 40–50% of the adult population and approximately 50–80% of adolescents. It is more frequently observed in women than in men. The severity of KP varies widely, ranging from minimal to severe cases. There are several subtypes of keratosis pilaris, including keratosis pilaris rubra (red, inflamed bumps), keratosis pilaris alba (rough, bumpy skin without irritation), and keratosis pilaris rubra faceii (reddish rash on the cheeks). Many individuals with keratosis pilaris may not even realize they have the condition, particularly if it is mild. While it may resemble goosebumps, KP is distinct in its presentation of small, rough bumps, which can often be confused with acne. Keratosis pilaris arises due to the accumulation of excess keratin, a natural protein in the skin, within the hair follicles. This process, known as hyperkeratinization, leads to the formation of hard plugs. The condition is primarily cosmetic and typically manifests as a proliferation of tiny, hard bumps that are rarely painful or itchy. Although KP persists year-round, it often worsens during colder months when ambient moisture levels are lower. During these times, the bumps may appear more pronounced in both color and texture. Many KP bumps contain an ingrown hair that has coiled within the follicle. This occurs because the keratinized skin caps off the hair follicle, preventing the hair from exiting. As a result, the hair grows inward, often encapsulated, and can sometimes be removed like an ingrown hair. However, removal may lead to scarring. There is currently no known cure for keratosis pilaris, but various treatments can effectively reduce the visibility of its symptoms. The condition often improves with age and may even resolve completely in adulthood, though some individuals may experience symptoms throughout their lives. Treatments are largely symptomatic and may require repeated application. Common approaches include exfoliation, the use of intensive moisturizing creams, and medicated lotions containing alpha hydroxy acids, urea, or retinoids like Retin-A. These treatments can temporarily improve the appearance and texture of the affected skin. Milk baths, which contain lactic acid (a natural alpha hydroxy acid), may also provide cosmetic benefits. Sunlight exposure may help alleviate symptoms for some individuals, but it carries an increased risk of skin cancer and can ultimately worsen the condition by drying out the skin. Oral vitamin A can be used in small amounts but must be approached with extreme caution due to its potential for liver toxicity. It is essential to consult a dermatologist or physician before taking additional vitamin A supplements. A safer and potentially effective treatment involves applying coconut oil to the affected areas, particularly during a shower. This may help reduce the bumps and, in some cases, prevent their recurrence. However, scratching or picking at KP bumps can cause redness, bleeding, and, in severe cases, scarring. Wearing loose-fitting clothing around affected areas can also help minimize irritation, as tight clothing (e.g., jeans) can exacerbate the condition through repeated friction, similar to scratching. Food allergies, particularly to gluten and dairy, may also aggravate keratosis pilaris by contributing to hyperkeratinization. While some individuals report that sun tanning alleviates symptoms, the associated risks of tanning, including an increased likelihood of skin cancer, may outweigh the benefits. In reality, sun exposure may temporarily improve the condition by breaking down the skin but can ultimately worsen it by causing dryness. The most effective approach is to use a cream or exfoliant that reduces the thickness of the skin while maintaining adequate hydration.
